meta.audience: Readers of the record of Zeniff
meta.location: The wilderness, then the land of Lehi-Nephi and Shilom
principles: A spy who changed his mind
A treaty that was a trap

world_behind.title: The abridgment stops and quotes
world_behind.text: "I, Zeniff" opens a document. Mormon has been compressing a thousand years; here he hands the narrative to a first-person source and keeps out of it for fourteen chapters. The chapter heading in the record calls it the record of Zeniff, and it reads like one.

world_behind.title: A spy who reports the wrong thing
world_behind.text: Sent to find weaknesses, Zeniff finds virtues. Israel's classic spy narrative sends twelve men into Canaan and the reports divide the nation; this sends one man among enemies and the report divides an army. The pattern is old and the reversal is the point.

world_behind.title: "Austere."
world_behind.text: The adjective occurs twice more in scripture, both in one parable, where a servant excuses himself by calling his master austere. Zeniff applies it to his own commander alongside blood-thirsty, and the pairing tells the reader what kind of man ordered his death.

world_behind.title: Two crops left untranslated
world_behind.text: Verse 9 lists corn, wheat, and barley, and then neas and sheum, neither of which occurs anywhere else in scripture and neither of which is rendered into English. A translation that has an equivalent uses it; these two apparently had none.

world_behind.title: A treaty designed to fail
world_behind.text: The king grants the land, empties the cities, and waits twelve years. Verse 10 tells the reader the purpose before the narrative reaches it. Vassal arrangements in the ancient world often worked exactly this way, and Zeniff writes it down as a man who found out afterward.

world_behind.title: Counted dead, on both sides
world_behind.text: Ancient battle reports round or inflate, and they rarely tally the victor's losses at all. This one gives an odd number for the enemy and a second odd number for the home side, and grieves over the second. The precision is itself the claim being made.

words.text: To observe secretly for military advantage. The word puts Zeniff in a recognizable Israelite role. Moses sent men to spy out Canaan and Joshua sent two into Jericho, and the whole chapter turns on what Zeniff does with the assignment. He completes the reconnaissance and refuses the conclusion.

Temper or inclination, what a person is disposed to do. Zeniff goes in to learn the king's disposition before committing his people, which is careful. That the answer he got was false is the chapter's bitterest irony, and the word will return in Mosiah 5 as the thing a changed heart alters.

The record's verb for what God does with his people, used here of a deal between two kings. Laman covenanted that Zeniff might possess Lehi-Nephi and Shilom, and the terms were kept: the Lamanites were ordered out and the cities changed hands. Scripture rarely lets this verb off God's side of an agreement, and the human cases it does allow keep hard company. Kishkumen's band had covenanted with him after a murder, and the chief priests covenanted with Judas for thirty pieces of silver. The word records that a promise was made. It says nothing about what the man making it was after.

Given as an explanation rather than an accusation. Zeniff pairs it with lazy and offers both as the reason the Lamanites wanted his people's labor. It is his account of a national character, written by a man at war with them, and the record preserves it as his view.

An army in formation, the King James word for a marshalled force. Zeniff uses it of the Lamanites who fall on farmers watering flocks, which sets a military term against an agricultural scene. The mismatch is the verse's whole account of what happened.

This record's spelling of scimitar, a curved blade, and a word the Bible does not have. It shows up only where weapons are being taken up or handed over, never in a description of daily life. What is worth noticing is whose hands hold it here. Zeniff is arming farmers, and the Lamanite host that comes over the hill in the next chapter carries the same inventory: bows, arrows, swords, cimeters, slings. Two peoples at war out of one armory.

phrases.term: When I saw that which was good among them I was desirous that they should not be destroyed
phrases.text: The turn happens in half a sentence and it happens because of observation. Zeniff does not report a revelation or a scruple; he reports seeing something good in people he had been sent to enable the killing of. The clause occurs once in scripture and it starts everything that follows.

phrases.term: He being an austere and a blood-thirsty man commanded that I should be slain
phrases.text: The disagreement is settled by an execution order. Zeniff had argued for a treaty; his commander's answer was to kill him. What follows, father against father and brother against brother, is the cost of that answer, and Zeniff records it in the same breath as his own rescue.

phrases.term: Father fought against father, and brother against brother
phrases.text: Civil war inside an army, described in the vocabulary the prophets use for a society coming apart. The phrase appears once in scripture. The greater number of the army died in it, and the survivors went home to tell the wives and children.

phrases.term: I being over-zealous to inherit the land of our fathers
phrases.text: Zeniff's judgment on himself, in the same word his grandson will use of him three generations later. It is the rare case where the record's verdict and the man's own agree exactly, and Zeniff writes it before describing the famine that followed.

phrases.term: For we were slow to remember the Lord our God
phrases.text: The reason attached to the famine, and it is offered without complaint. Zeniff is narrating his own expedition and assigns the suffering to his own party's forgetfulness. The phrase runs through this record and this is where it enters.

Two crops in a list of five, and the only two the translation does not render. Corn, wheat, and barley have English names; these do not. The verse is a farmer's inventory and it preserves two words that came through the process untouched.

phrases.term: It was the cunning and the craftiness of king Laman, to bring my people into bondage
phrases.text: The narrator telling the reader the plot before the characters discover it. Zeniff is writing years later and places the explanation next to the grant of land. Everything in verses 6 through 9 reads differently once this sentence has been read.

phrases.term: That they might glut themselves with the labors of our hands
phrases.text: Bondage described as an appetite. The verb belongs with drunkenness and gluttony in the King James Bible, and applying it to a labor arrangement makes the tribute a matter of consumption. The next clause continues it: feast themselves upon the flocks.

phrases.term: All manner of weapons which we could invent
phrases.text: To invent is to devise or contrive, not to imagine, and the clause concedes that the list before it was improvised. Six weapon types named, then an admission that the colony was not armed and had to think of something. Bows, arrows, swords, cimeters, clubs, slings. Some of these are likely farm tools with a use found for them. Zeniff is describing a civilian population arming itself in a hurry.

phrases.term: We were awakened to a remembrance of the deliverance of our fathers
phrases.text: The memory arrives under attack. Zeniff had just said his people were slow to remember; here the remembering finally happens, and what they remember is a rescue. The strength they go out in is borrowed from a story.

phrases.term: I, myself, with mine own hands, did help to bury their dead
phrases.text: A king burying the enemy. Two intensifiers on the pronoun, the same construction Mosiah used of tilling his own ground, and the object of the labor is three thousand corpses. Zeniff reports it in one clause and then counts his own losses.

verses.label: v. 1–2
verses.title: The spy, and the mutiny
verses.text: Taught in the language, knowing the land, sent to find military weakness, and finding good instead. He argues for a treaty; the commander orders him killed; he is rescued at the cost of a battle inside the army; most of the force dies; the survivors go home to tell the families. Two verses, and they contain a whole war.

verses.label: v. 3–4
verses.title: The second attempt
verses.text: Over-zealous by his own account, he gathers volunteers and goes back. Famine and sore afflictions, because they were slow to remember God. Many days of wandering, and then tents pitched at the site where the first expedition's dead were left.

verses.label: v. 5–9
verses.title: The grant, and the building
verses.text: Four men into the city to read the king's temper; a covenant granting Lehi-Nephi and Shilom; the Lamanites ordered out; walls repaired, buildings raised, ground tilled with corn, wheat, barley, neas, sheum, and fruit. Five verses of a colony working, and every one of them is about to be undercut.

verses.label: v. 10–13
verses.title: What the grant was for
verses.text: Cunning and craftiness; twelve years of watching a colony grow strong; a king made uneasy; a people described as lazy and idolatrous who wanted the labor of other people's hands; and then agitation, wars, and contentions. The trap takes twelve years to close.

verses.label: v. 14–16
verses.title: The attack
verses.text: The thirteenth year, south of Shilom, people watering flocks and tilling fields, a numerous host falling on them, flocks and corn taken. Survivors flee to the city and call on Zeniff for protection, and he arms them with whatever can be improvised.

verses.label: v. 17–18
verses.title: The battle
verses.text: They cried mightily, remembered the deliverance of their fathers, went out in the strength of the Lord, and killed three thousand and forty-three in a day and a night, driving the rest out. God heard, and the record says so before it says who won.

verses.label: v. 19
verses.title: The burial
verses.text: He helped bury the enemy dead with his own hands, and then gives his own casualty count. One verse for the aftermath, and it is the only sentence in the chapter with sorrow in it.

chapter.title: A first-person record inside an abridgment
chapter.text: Mormon steps aside and lets Zeniff talk. The change of voice is not announced beyond the opening pronoun, and it changes what the reader can know. For fourteen chapters the account has the limits and the interests of the man writing it, including his self-assessments.

chapter.title: The turn happens through observation
chapter.text: Zeniff was sent to find weakness and saw good. Nothing supernatural intervenes. The record's account of how an enemy stops being an enemy is that somebody looked closely enough to notice something worth preserving.

chapter.title: He convicts himself in his own document
chapter.text: Over-zealous, slow to remember, deceived by a treaty he negotiated. Limhi will say the same things about him in the previous chapter of the reader's experience, and the reader arrives at Zeniff's account already knowing the verdict, then finds the defendant agreeing with it.

chapter.title: The narrator spoils his own plot
chapter.text: Verse 10 explains the trap before the trap springs. The account is not built for suspense; it reads as an explanation for descendants who are living in the consequences. The structure tells you who the document was for.

chapter.title: The Lamanite characterization is his, and the record keeps it labeled
chapter.text: Lazy, idolatrous, wanting to glut themselves on other people's labor: this is a colonist at war describing the people whose land he was granted. The record has already given the reader Jacob 3, where the same people are called more righteous than the Nephites.

chapter.title: The battle report ends in a graveyard
chapter.text: Three thousand and forty-three enemies, two hundred and seventy-nine of his own, a king with a shovel, and the words "great sorrow and lamentation." Whatever the chapter is celebrating, it stops celebrating in the last verse.

applications.title: Look before you conclude
applications.text: Zeniff was sent to confirm a judgment and looked closely enough to overturn it. Take a group you have already decided about and spend real attention on what is good among them.

applications.title: Say the honest word about yourself
applications.text: He wrote "over-zealous" about his own motive, in his own record. Name the good motive of yours that has been running past its bounds, in the same plain terms someone else would use.

applications.title: Notice the grant that costs nothing to give
applications.text: The land was handed over because handing it over served someone's purpose. When something arrives easily, ask who benefits from your having it.

applications.title: Remember under pressure
applications.text: They were slow to remember until they were attacked, and then the memory was a rescue story. Decide now which deliverance you will reach for, so it is there when you need it.

applications.title: Bury the dead yourself
applications.text: Zeniff did the work with his own hands, for enemies. After a conflict you have won, do one concrete thing that costs you and honors the other side.

applications.title: Count both columns
applications.text: He recorded his enemies' losses and his own, and grieved for one. Whatever you are keeping score of, write down what it cost as well as what it gained.

questions.text: Whose good have I refused to look at because of what noticing it would require of me?
When I was overruled harshly, what did it cost the people around me?
What am I over-zealous about that I would defend as simply faithful?
What have I been given that I should have been more suspicious of?
Am I slow to remember, and what wakes me up?
Do I grieve the cost of the things I win?
